articles.excerpt: You have been told a book is free. You clicked through, saw a cover image and the word "Read", and either hit a paywall three paragraphs in or got forty pages of a two-hundred-page book and a "buy" bu…
articles.body: You have been told a book is free. You clicked through, saw a cover image and the word "Read", and either hit a paywall three paragraphs in or got forty pages of a two-hundred-page book and a "buy" button. You downloaded it anyway, and it now sits in a folder called PDFs you have not opened since. You have done this eleven times. The problem is not that free books are hard to find. It is that "free" and "available" are the same thing, and they are not. Libraries are full of records: metadata about books you cannot download, catalogue entries for titles whose only copy sits in a reading room in Boston, and links that resolve to a lending queue rather than a file.

articles.title: 7 Google Ads Mistakes That Are Draining Local Business Budgets (And How to Fix Them)
articles.excerpt: The average small local business wastes between 40% and 60% of their Google Ads budget on clicks that will never convert. I've audited hundreds of local campaigns, and the same seven mistakes show up…
articles.body: The average small local business wastes between 40% and 60% of their Google Ads budget on clicks that will never convert. I've audited hundreds of local campaigns, and the same seven mistakes show up every single time — whether it's a $300/month HVAC company or a $5,000/month dental group. Here's what's burning your money, and exactly what to do about it today. Mistake #1: Running on Broad Match With No Negative Keywords This is the #1 budget killer for local businesses, and it's shockingly common. When you add a keyword like plumber on broad match, Google is free to show your ad for searches like "plumber salary," "plumber licensing school," and "how to become a licensed plumber." You'll pay for every click — and none of those visitors want to hire you.

articles.title: 10 digits or 13? The timestamp bug that sends your dates to the year 56,189
articles.excerpt: Every API you have ever used stores time as one number: the seconds since January 1, 1970. Databases do it, JWT tokens do it, log files do it. The number is timezone-free and sortable, which is why ev…
articles.body: Every API you have ever used stores time as one number: the seconds since January 1, 1970. Databases do it, JWT tokens do it, log files do it. The number is timezone-free and sortable, which is why everyone uses it. And then one day your UI shows a date in the year 56,189, and you spend an hour looking for a bug that is exactly one multiplication away. The bug is units. A Unix timestamp in seconds has 10 digits: 1700000000. A JavaScript timestamp in milliseconds has 13 digits: 1700000000000. JavaScript's Date.now() returns milliseconds. Most APIs return seconds. Feed a millisecond value into code that expects seconds and new Date(1700000000000 * 1000) lands tens of thousands of years in the future.

articles.title: PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificates have the same fix: rebuild the image
articles.excerpt: I'll admit something slightly embarrassing. For years my mental model of a compromised certificate was "the browsers will handle it." Somebody revokes it, Chrome and Firefox stop trusting it, and I go…
articles.body: I'll admit something slightly embarrassing. For years my mental model of a compromised certificate was "the browsers will handle it." Somebody revokes it, Chrome and Firefox stop trusting it, and I go back to watching my build. That model has a hole in it, and the hole is shaped exactly like every container I ship. Docker's write-up on PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise is the clearest explanation of that hole I've read in a while. Two unrelated security events landed in the same week. If you run containers, both come down to the same chore of rebuilding the image on a fixed base and redeploying it. Two incidents, one chore PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

articles.title: How I built sub-agents for my desktop AI companion: isolated children, one capped envelope, and no grandchildren
articles.excerpt: Ankita is my open-source desktop AI companion — a little companion, a lot more possible. It lives on my machine, runs on my models, and does real work in my workspace: reading code, editing files, run…
articles.body: Ankita is my open-source desktop AI companion — a little companion, a lot more possible. It lives on my machine, runs on my models, and does real work in my workspace: reading code, editing files, running checks. Sooner or later, any agent like that hits the same wall: one conversation trying to do three independent jobs at once. The parent's context balloons, the work interleaves, and a long task blocks everything behind it. The obvious fix is sub-agents — hand a piece of work to a child. The dangerous version is giving the child everything the parent has. I built the opposite: a child that gets almost nothing, runs its own tool loop, and comes back with exactly one capped envelope.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.body: Credit: NASA The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.   “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks for the ceremony. “NASA and the Vietnam National Space Center have built momentum in satellite innovation, land-use research, and radar-based Earth observation. Joining the Artemis Accords opens a new chapter in that relationship. We’ve aligned on the principles. The opportunities are in front of us, and now we can build on that foundation together.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.
